proposedTopics.title: Reentrancy attacks
proposedTopics.description: The archetypal external-call bug family: a contract calls out to an address that re-enters it before its own state is updated, so a stale balance or flag is trusted twice. Spans single-function, cross-function, cross-contract, read-only, and callback-hook variants; defenses include restoring invariants before external calls and applying a shared reentrancy guard where needed.

proposedTopics.title: Access control & authorization attacks
proposedTopics.description: OWASP SC01 in the current Smart Contract Top 10: functions that fail to check who is calling, or check it wrongly. Missing modifiers, tx.origin authorization, unprotected initializers or privileged opcodes, and weak signature checks can all let an attacker invoke privileged logic.

proposedTopics.title: Arithmetic & precision attacks
proposedTopics.description: Bugs where the math is the vulnerability: overflow or underflow (pre-0.8 or inside unchecked arithmetic, casts, or assembly), premature integer division, wrong rounding direction, and share-price manipulation in vaults. Small rounding edges can compound into drainable value.

proposedTopics.title: Price oracle & flash-loan attacks
proposedTopics.description: OWASP SC03/SC04: an attacker distorts the price or voting power a protocol reads — a spot AMM reserve, a weak TWAP, or a current-balance governance vote — often funding the distortion with a single-transaction flash loan. Root cause is trusting state that temporary borrowed liquidity can rewrite.

proposedTopics.title: Single-function reentrancy
proposedTopics.description: A withdraw() that sends ETH via a low-level call before zeroing the caller's recorded balance lets the recipient's receive()/fallback re-enter withdraw() and drain the contract, because the balance check still passes on each re-entry. The 2016 DAO attack recursively called its split path and drained more than 3.6 million ETH, prompting the DAO fork. Fix the stale-state window with Checks-Effects-Interactions and, where appropriate, a reentrancy guard.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in security/attacks/reentrancy-single/ write a vulnerable Vault (balance decremented AFTER the call), an Attacker that re-enters withdraw() from receive() to drain it, and a Foundry test that proves the drain; then apply CEI + OpenZeppelin ReentrancyGuard. Done when: the exploit test empties the vault on the vulnerable contract and reverts after the fix.

requirements.purpose: Trace the inconsistent-state window and apply Checks-Effects-Interactions without relying on a gas stipend

proposedTopics.title: Cross-function & cross-contract reentrancy
proposedTopics.description: Guarding only one entry point is not enough when another function or contract can observe the same inconsistent state: the attacker re-enters an unguarded function that reads the not-yet-updated balance, or bounces through a second contract outside the lock. The shared invariant, not one named function, must hold before control leaves the system.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in security/attacks/reentrancy-cross/ write a contract with withdraw() and transfer() sharing a balances mapping, where transfer() has no guard; the Attacker re-enters transfer() mid-withdraw to move a stale balance. Done when: the test double-spends on the vulnerable version and fails once CEI is applied across BOTH functions.

requirements.purpose: Reason about reentrancy as an invariant boundary spanning entry points and contracts

options.why: OpenZeppelin frames the bug around observable inconsistent invariants and documents the shared guard semantics needed across relevant entry points.

proposedTopics.title: Read-only reentrancy
proposedTopics.description: A view function writes no state, yet an attacker can call it mid-manipulation: during a callback such as Curve's ETH-paying remove_liquidity path, pool balances and LP supply can be temporarily inconsistent, so get_virtual_price() reports a wrong value that an integrating contract trusts. The 2022 disclosure exposed several major integrations. Fix the read path or reject reads while the upstream pool's lock is entered.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in security/attacks/reentrancy-readonly/ write a Pool whose ETH-refund path is reentrant and a Consumer that prices collateral from the pool's view function; the Attacker re-enters during remove-liquidity and borrows against a corrupted price. Done when: the test over-borrows on the vulnerable consumer and reverts after the read is guarded by the pool's reentrancy lock.

requirements.purpose: Reproduce the temporary Curve balance-versus-supply inconsistency and its effect on a view consumer

proposedTopics.title: ERC-777 & callback-hook reentrancy
proposedTopics.description: Tokens with transfer hooks — ERC-777 tokensToSend/tokensReceived, ERC-1155 onERC1155Received, and ERC-721 onERC721Received — execute external code during a transfer. A caller that assumes an ERC-20-compatible transfer is inert can therefore expose stale accounting; the disclosed Uniswap V1/ERC-777 vulnerability used this compatibility edge. Restore invariants before the hook can observe them and use a guard where necessary.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in security/attacks/reentrancy-erc777/ write an exchange that pays ETH before calling transferFrom on an ERC-777-compatible token, and an Attacker whose tokensToSend hook re-enters the sale while the ETH reserve is already lower but the token reserve is stale. Done when: repeated hook-driven sales extract excess ETH on the vulnerable exchange and fail once reserve/accounting effects precede the interaction and the entry point is guarded.

proposedTopics.title: Missing & incorrect access-control modifiers
proposedTopics.description: A state-changing or fund-moving function is externally reachable without the intended owner or role check, or checks the wrong role, letting an unauthorized caller invoke privileged logic. Fix the authorization at every privileged entry point and audit the complete external/public function surface against the intended role matrix.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in security/attacks/access-missing/ write a Vault whose setOwner()/sweep() is public with no modifier, and a test where a non-owner EOA seizes ownership and drains it; then add onlyOwner and re-run. Done when: the attacker call succeeds pre-fix and reverts with the access error post-fix.

proposedTopics.title: tx.origin authentication
proposedTopics.description: Authenticating with `tx.origin == owner` instead of `msg.sender == owner` is phishable: if the owner is tricked into calling a malicious contract, that contract calls the victim, and tx.origin is still the owner, so the check passes. Authorize the immediate caller with msg.sender.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in security/attacks/tx-origin/ write a Wallet gated by tx.origin, a malicious Lure contract, and a test where the owner calling Lure triggers a transfer out of the Wallet; then switch the check to msg.sender. Done when: the phishing test drains the wallet pre-fix and reverts post-fix.

requirements.purpose: Distinguish transaction origin from the immediate message caller in an authorization check

proposedTopics.title: Uninitialized proxy & unprotected initializer
proposedTopics.description: Proxy deployments move setup from the implementation's constructor to an initializer executed in proxy storage. If initialization is omitted or repeatable, an attacker can claim ownership of the proxy; if the implementation is left initializable, it can be taken over directly and may endanger the proxy. Use a one-shot initializer, initialize the proxy atomically, and call _disableInitializers() in the implementation constructor.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in security/attacks/uninit-proxy/ write an upgradeable Vault whose initialize() sets owner but lacks the initializer guard, and a test where an attacker calls initialize() to claim ownership; then add the guard + _disableInitializers(). Done when: the attacker becomes owner pre-fix and initialize() reverts as already-initialized post-fix.

requirements.purpose: Protect proxy initialization and separately lock the implementation contract

proposedTopics.title: Unprotected selfdestruct
proposedTopics.description: An unguarded path to SELFDESTRUCT lets any caller force the contract's entire ETH balance to the chosen beneficiary. Since Cancun/EIP-6780, it does not delete code or storage unless executed in the same transaction as creation, but the balance transfer and execution halt remain; the opcode is deprecated and new uses are strongly discouraged. Avoid it, or strictly authorize any unavoidable legacy path.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in security/attacks/selfdestruct/ write a funded Bank with an unguarded kill(address payable beneficiary), and test under Cancun semantics that an attacker can force its full ETH balance to the attacker while the pre-existing contract's code remains. Done when: the unauthorized balance transfer succeeds pre-fix and reverts after onlyOwner is added; separately assert the code-preservation behavior required by EIP-6780.

requirements.purpose: Test the current balance-transfer and code-preservation semantics of SELFDESTRUCT

proposedTopics.title: Signature-based authorization gaps
proposedTopics.description: When authorization is proven by an off-chain signature instead of msg.sender, the contract must recover a nonzero signer, verify that signer has the required role, and hash the intended structured action under the correct domain. Merely recovering some address proves signature validity, not authorization; replay and malleability are covered separately under signature attacks.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in security/attacks/sig-authz/ write an admin action gated by an ECDSA signature that forgets to check the recovered signer against an allowlist; a test authorizes with an arbitrary key. Done when: the unauthorized signer executes the action pre-fix and is rejected once the signer allowlist check is added.

requirements.purpose: Recover a signer under the intended domain and then enforce the signer's role explicitly

options.scope: Sections ECDSA, MessageHashUtils, and EIP712
options.why: The current API separates signer recovery, message hashing, and typed-data domains, making clear that the application must still check the recovered account's authority.

proposedTopics.title: Integer overflow & underflow
proposedTopics.description: Before Solidity 0.8 arithmetic wrapped silently; Solidity 0.8+ reverts on ordinary overflow and underflow by default. The protection does not make unchecked arithmetic, explicit narrowing conversions, or inline assembly safe: unchecked operations wrap and explicit integer conversions truncate. Keep value-bearing arithmetic checked and use range-checked casts such as SafeCast.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in security/attacks/overflow/ write a token whose transfer subtracts inside an unchecked block (and a uint96 downcast on amount), and a test where an underflow/truncation mints or steals balance; then remove unchecked and add SafeCast. Done when: the exploit inflates a balance pre-fix and reverts post-fix.

requirements.purpose: Identify where Solidity 0.8 checks end and wrapping or truncation resumes

options.why: The compiler documentation defines checked defaults, unchecked wrapping, and truncating explicit conversions used by the vulnerable token.

requirements.purpose: Replace a silent narrowing conversion with a checked downcast

proposedTopics.title: Division-before-multiplication & precision loss
proposedTopics.description: Solidity integer division rounds toward zero, so `(a / b) * c` discards a remainder before the multiplication can preserve it. Moving multiplication first may overflow even when the final quotient fits, so use full-precision mulDiv where necessary and choose the rounding direction for the economic operation explicitly. Repeated favorable rounding can turn small errors into extractable value.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in security/attacks/precision/ write a reward/fee calculation that divides before multiplying and rounds in the attacker's favor, and a Foundry test that repeats the operation to extract value or underpay; then use Math.mulDiv with the intended rounding mode. Done when: the test shows a non-zero cumulative edge pre-fix and no attacker-favorable residue post-fix.

requirements.purpose: Predict when integer division discards precision and choose an explicit rounding direction

requirements.purpose: Compute multiplication and division without avoidable intermediate overflow

proposedTopics.title: ERC-4626 first-depositor share inflation
proposedTopics.description: In a naive empty ERC-4626 vault, a first depositor can mint a tiny share amount and then donate underlying directly, raising totalAssets without minting shares. A later deposit can round down to zero shares, after which the attacker redeems the victim's assets. OpenZeppelin's defense combines virtual assets and shares with a decimals offset, making the attack unprofitable while reducing rounding loss.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in security/attacks/vault-inflation/ write a naive ERC-4626 (assets = token.balanceOf(this)) and a test: attacker deposits 1 wei, donates a large amount, victim deposits and gets 0 shares, attacker redeems the lot; then switch to OZ's virtual-offset vault. Done when: the victim is robbed pre-fix and gets fair shares post-fix.

requirements.purpose: Quantify the donation attack and the loss captured by virtual assets and shares

proposedTopics.title: Token decimals mismatch
proposedTopics.description: Assuming every token has 18 decimals breaks integrations with assets such as 6-decimal USDC or 8-decimal WBTC: the same human amount has a different integer representation. Normalize each explicitly supported asset using verified integration metadata; ERC-20 decimals() is optional, so arbitrary token-supplied metadata is not a trust boundary by itself.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in security/attacks/decimals/ write a two-token exchange that hardcodes 1e18 scaling and a test that swaps a configured 6-decimal token to extract 10^12x value; then normalize with immutable per-asset scale factors validated when the supported tokens are configured. Done when: the mis-scaled swap over-pays pre-fix and is balanced post-fix.

requirements.purpose: Treat token decimals as representation metadata and account for its optional status

options.scope: Sections Token, Methods, and decimals
options.why: The canonical standard defines decimals as a display divisor and explicitly marks the method optional, supporting configured rather than blindly trusted scaling.

proposedTopics.title: Spot-price oracle manipulation
proposedTopics.description: Pricing collateral from an AMM's instantaneous reserves means one large swap can move the reported price for exactly as long as an attacker needs it. They skew the pool, borrow or mint against the false price, and unwind the trade, leaving the consumer with bad debt. Do not use a manipulable pool's spot reserves as an independent price oracle.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in security/attacks/oracle-spot/ deploy a constant-product pool and a Lender that prices collateral from spot reserves; a test swaps to move the price, over-borrows, and swaps back. Done when: the attacker extracts more than deposited pre-fix and the borrow is bounded once priced off a TWAP/Chainlink mock.

proposedTopics.title: TWAP oracle manipulation
proposedTopics.description: A time-weighted average price raises the cost of a momentary move, but it is not immune: a short window or low-liquidity market can still be held away from fair value long enough to move the average. A longer window costs more to manipulate but responds more slowly to real market changes, so observation period, liquidity assumptions, and fallback behavior are security parameters.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in security/attacks/oracle-twap/ implement a Uniswap-V2-style cumulative-price TWAP and a consumer, then a multi-block Foundry test (vm.roll/vm.warp) that walks the average on a thin pool enough to over-borrow. Done when: the test moves the TWAP past the consumer's safety margin on a low-liquidity setup and fails once the window/liquidity floor is raised.

proposedTopics.title: Flash-loan price manipulation
proposedTopics.description: A flash loan supplies large temporary liquidity for one atomic transaction: borrow, act, and repay, or the transaction reverts. That can remove much of the attacker's upfront-capital requirement for spot-oracle manipulation. Harvest Finance's first-party account describes a 2020 flash-loan-funded economic attack against manipulated Curve pool valuation; the loan amplified the vulnerable price/accounting design.

Done when: the single-tx exploit nets profit against the spot-priced lender and is unprofitable once the lender uses a resistant oracle.

proposedTopics.title: Flash-loan governance attacks
proposedTopics.description: If voting power is read from a current balance or an attacker-controlled snapshot, borrowed tokens can satisfy a proposal threshold or quorum temporarily. In 2022, Beanstalk reported that a flash loan compromised its governance mechanism and stole about $77M in non-Beanstalk user assets. Past-timepoint vote checkpoints, voting delay, and a separate execution timelock narrow this class of attack.

proposedTopics.title: Stale & misconfigured price feeds
proposedTopics.description: A correctly operated data feed can still be unsafe for a particular consumer if the contract ignores updatedAt, assumes the wrong response decimals, uses the wrong feed or network, or has no behavior for unavailable data. proposedTopics.title: Read-only reentrancy into oracles
proposedTopics.description: The oracle-focused read-only reentrancy variant occurs when a consumer prices assets from a pool view while the pool is mid-callback and its balances and share supply are transiently inconsistent. ChainSecurity's 2022 Curve disclosure showed get_virtual_price() could be manipulated and identified multiple exposed integrations. Reject reads while the upstream lock is entered—probing a harmless lock-protected function when the lock is not public—or use a source whose invariants hold during callbacks.

Model the historical consumer fix by calling a harmless lock-protected pool function immediately before the price read. Done when: the over-borrow succeeds pre-fix and reverts because that probe encounters the entered lock after the fix.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why does a withdraw() that transfers ETH before zeroing the caller's balance let an attacker drain the contract?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: The external call hands control to the attacker's receive()/fallback while their recorded balance is still non-zero, so they re-call withdraw() and pass the same balance check repeatedly before it is ever decremented. Fix: Checks-Effects-Interactions (zero the balance BEFORE the call) plus a nonReentrant mutex. Pitfall: relying on .transfer's 2300-gas stipend to block reentrancy is fragile — gas costs shift across forks; fix the ordering, not the gas.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write the Checks-Effects-Interactions fix for a reentrant ETH withdraw().
proposedPrompts.answerHint: function withdraw() external nonReentrant { uint256 bal = balance[msg.sender]; require(bal > 0); balance[msg.sender] = 0; (bool ok, ) = msg.sender.call{value: bal}(""); require(ok); } // effect (zeroing) precedes interaction (call)

proposedPrompts.promptText: Ethernaut level 10 (Re-entrancy): drain the target contract's entire balance.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Deploy an attacker that donates via donate(), calls withdraw() for that amount, and in receive() re-enters withdraw() while the target still credits the stale balance — loop until the target is empty, then collect. The bug is state updated after the send.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why can a per-function nonReentrant guard still leave a contract reentrant?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: If only one entry point is guarded, a second function or sibling contract that reads or writes the same state may remain callable during the external interaction. The attacker re-enters that unguarded path and acts on stale state. Reentrancy is a property of shared invariants across the system: restore them before the call and cover all relevant entry points with the same lock boundary.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Damn Vulnerable DeFi — Side Entrance: drain the pool that lets you deposit inside a flash-loan callback.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Take a flash loan, and in the callback deposit the borrowed ETH back into the same pool (satisfying the balance check) — the loan is 'repaid' while crediting you a balance; then withdraw() it. It's cross-function reentrancy: flashLoan and deposit/withdraw share one ETH balance with no consistent guard.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How can a view function with no state to guard still be part of a reentrancy exploit?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: It is read DURING a reentrant callback, while the contract's internal accounting is transiently inconsistent (e.g. Curve mid remove_liquidity that sends ETH): the view returns a wrong price/virtual-price that a consumer trusts as ground truth. Pitfall: adding a nonReentrant guard to state-changing functions doesn't protect external READERS — the pool must expose (or the consumer must check) its reentrancy lock on the read path too.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Damn Vulnerable DeFi — Curvy Puppet: exploit the read-only reentrancy in the Curve-based price source.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Trigger a Curve callback (ETH refund) and, while the pool's accounting is mid-update, have the lending contract read the corrupted virtual price to liquidate/borrow on wrong terms. The fix is checking Curve's reentrancy lock before reading the price.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why does an ERC-777 (or ERC-1155/721 receiver) token turn a normally-safe transfer into a reentrancy vector?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: These standards invoke external hooks during a transfer: ERC-777 calls the sender's tokensToSend before updating balances and the recipient's tokensReceived afterward, while ERC-1155/ERC-721 call receiver hooks. That hands control to attacker code while the integrating contract may still have unfinished accounting. Pitfall: 'it's just an ERC-20 integration' is wrong if a compatible token has hooks; apply CEI plus a guard and constrain arbitrary token lists.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Replay the Cream Finance / imBTC-style ERC-777 reentrancy from DeFiHackLabs and reproduce the drain locally.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Mock an ERC-20-compatible ERC-777 and register the attacker's tokensToSend hook. Sell tokens to an exchange that pays ETH before transferFrom; re-enter the sale from tokensToSend, after the ETH reserve has fallen but before the token reserve changes. Repeated micro-sales extract more ETH than non-reentrant sales. Move accounting effects before the interaction and guard the entry point.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What is the access-control failure mode, and why is it OWASP SC01 (the top loss category)?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A fund-moving or state-changing function ships with default public/external visibility and no (or a wrong-role) modifier, so any address can call it — seize ownership, mint, sweep, upgrade. It tops the list because it needs no clever mechanism, just one unguarded privileged entry point, and it directly moves funds. Pitfall: 'internal-only' intent isn't enforcement — if it's reachable and unguarded, it's public; enumerate every privileged function and prove each has a check.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write an onlyOwner modifier and show it applied to a privileged sweep().
proposedPrompts.answerHint: modifier onlyOwner() { require(msg.sender == owner, "not owner"); _; } function sweep(address to) external onlyOwner { (bool ok,) = to.call{value: address(this).balance}(""); require(ok); }

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why is `require(tx.origin == owner)` phishable, and what should replace it?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: tx.origin is the EOA that started the whole tx, not the immediate caller; if the owner is lured into calling a malicious contract, that contract calls the victim and tx.origin is STILL the owner, so the check passes. Replace with `msg.sender == owner`, which authorizes the direct caller. Pitfall: the only legitimate uses of tx.origin are niche (e.g. refund-to-origin, anti-contract heuristics) — never for authorization.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Ethernaut — Telephone: claim ownership of a contract that checks tx.origin != msg.sender.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Call the target THROUGH an intermediary contract: your EOA calls your contract (tx.origin = you), which calls changeOwner (msg.sender = your contract), so tx.origin != msg.sender holds and you become owner. Demonstrates why tx.origin is not identity.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why is an unprotected initialize() dangerous in an upgradeable contract, and how is it fixed?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Proxies can't run the implementation's constructor, so setup moves to initialize(); if it lacks a one-shot guard, an attacker calls it first (or front-runs deploy) to set themselves as owner. Fix: OpenZeppelin `initializer` modifier (reverts on a repeated call), initialize atomically with deployment, and call _disableInitializers() in the implementation's constructor so the logic contract can't be initialized directly. Pitfall: proxy storage and implementation storage are separate trust boundaries; protect both.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Ethernaut — Puzzle Wallet: exploit the proxy whose storage layout lets you become owner via init/deposit.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: The proxy (PuzzleProxy) and wallet share storage slots, so setting pendingAdmin collides with the wallet's owner; call proposeNewAdmin/init to align slots, use the multicall to double-count a deposit, drain, then take admin — a storage-collision + initialization bug.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What damage does an unguarded selfdestruct do, and what happened to Parity?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: In the 2017 Parity incident, an attacker initialized the shared wallet library and called its kill path; under the pre-Cancun rules that deleted the library code and froze wallets that depended on it. Under post-Cancun EIP-6780, SELFDESTRUCT on a pre-existing contract instead transfers its full ETH balance and leaves code/storage intact; deletion remains only in the creation transaction. Avoid the deprecated opcode or strictly authorize the path.

proposedPrompts.promptText: When authorization is proven by an off-chain signature, what must the contract check to avoid privilege escalation?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: That ecrecover returned a NON-zero address that is in the authorized signer set (not just 'a valid signature'), and that the signed message is bound to this contract, chain, function, and a nonce/deadline so it can't be reused or forged. Pitfall: ecrecover returns address(0) for malformed signatures — if address(0) is ever a privileged/uninitialized signer, an attacker submits garbage and passes; always reject the zero address explicitly.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Where do overflow/underflow bugs still occur in Solidity 0.8+, given arithmetic reverts by default?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Inside `unchecked { }` blocks (used for gas), in explicit downcasts (uint256→uint128/uint96 silently truncate), and in inline assembly / Yul (no checks at all) — the default protection doesn't reach any of those. Pitfall: `unchecked` for a loop counter is fine, but wrapping a balance subtraction or a cast on user-controlled amounts reintroduces the classic wrap; validate ranges before casting and prefer SafeCast.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Show a downcast that silently truncates a user amount and the SafeCast fix.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: // BUG: uint96 packed = uint96(amount); // amount > 2^96-1 wraps silently\nuint96 packed = SafeCast.toUint96(amount); // reverts if amount doesn't fit

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why does `(a / b) * c` lose value that `(a * c) / b` keeps, and how does rounding direction matter?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Solidity integer division rounds toward zero, so dividing first discards precision before a later multiply can use it. Multiplying first can overflow even when the quotient fits, so use a full-precision mulDiv implementation when needed. Choose an explicit rounding mode for the economic operation and test that repeated rounding cannot systematically favor the caller.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Walk through the ERC-4626 first-depositor / donation inflation attack and its standard mitigation.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: On an empty vault the attacker mints a tiny number of shares, then transfers underlying straight to the vault so totalAssets rises while totalSupply does not. The victim's deposit rounds down to zero shares, effectively donating assets that the attacker can redeem. OpenZeppelin's defense adds virtual assets and shares plus a decimals offset; the offset improves precision and the virtual balances capture part of the attacker's donation, making the attack unprofitable.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Show the vulnerable share-minting line and the virtual-offset idea that fixes it.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: // BUG: shares = totalSupply == 0 ? assets : assets * totalSupply / token.balanceOf(address(this));\n// FIX (OZ): use virtual shares+assets offset so an empty vault can't be inflated: convert with (totalSupply + 10**offset) and (totalAssets + 1).

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does assuming 18 decimals create an exploitable bug when integrating USDC or WBTC?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: USDC/USDT use 6 decimals and WBTC 8, so a hardcoded 1e18 scale can mis-value raw amounts by 10^12 or 10^10. Normalize supported assets with configured, verified scale factors. ERC-20 decimals() is optional and arbitrary tokens may omit or misreport it, so validate metadata as part of the integration rather than trusting each caller-supplied token.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why is an AMM's spot reserve ratio an unsafe price oracle?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Spot price = current reserves, and a single swap changes the reserves for exactly as long as the attacker needs; they skew the pool, borrow/mint against the false price in the same block, then swap back and profit. The pool is an oracle anyone with (flash-loaned) capital can rewrite. Fix: price off a manipulation-resistant source — Chainlink, or a sufficiently long TWAP with a liquidity floor. Pitfall: 'we use an on-chain DEX price, so it's decentralized' confuses decentralization with manipulation-resistance.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Ethernaut — Dex: drain one token from the AMM by exploiting its price formula.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: The Dex prices swaps as (amount * toReserve / fromReserve) with integer truncation; by swapping the full balance back and forth you push the ratio further each time until one side rounds in your favor and you can take the entire reserve of a token. It's on-chain-price manipulation via the pool's own formula.

proposedPrompts.promptText: A TWAP resists single-block manipulation — so what is still the attacker's angle, and what is the design tradeoff?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: On a thin pool or short observation window, an attacker can hold the market away from fair value long enough to drag the average. Lengthening the period raises manipulation cost but makes the oracle lag real price changes. Security therefore depends on liquidity and observation assumptions as well as window length, with explicit fallback behavior when those assumptions fail.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What does a flash loan add to an oracle-manipulation attack, and where is the real bug?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A flash loan supplies large temporary liquidity for one atomic transaction (repay by transaction end or the whole transaction reverts), sharply reducing the attacker's upfront-capital requirement. They skew a spot oracle, exploit the false price, repay, and keep the remainder. The root bug is the manipulable price source; blocking known lenders does not fix it.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Damn Vulnerable DeFi — Puppet: drain the lending pool that prices collateral from a Uniswap spot pool.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: The pool computes required collateral from the Uniswap V1 (or V2) spot price; dump a large amount of the token into Uniswap to crater its price, then borrow the pool's entire token balance for almost no collateral. Puppet V2/V3 raise the bar (V2 pair, V3 TWAP window) but reduce to the same manipulable-price root.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does a flash loan defeat token-balance-based governance, and what stops it?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: If voting power is read from a current balance or attacker-controlled snapshot, borrowed tokens can satisfy quorum temporarily and be repaid after execution. Beanstalk reported about $77M in non-Beanstalk user assets stolen through its governance mechanism. Use past-timepoint ERC20Votes checkpoints, a voting delay, and a separate execution timelock; a snapshot created after borrowing is not protection.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Damn Vulnerable DeFi — Selfie: pass a malicious governance action using a flash-loaned snapshot.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Flash-borrow the governance token, call snapshot() so your borrowed balance is recorded as voting power, queue a proposal that drains the pool via emergencyExit/drainAllFunds, repay the loan, then after the action delay execute it. The bug is voting power taken from a snapshot the attacker controls within the loan.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What must a Chainlink consumer validate on latestRoundData(), and why?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Require a positive answer, normalize using the feed's decimals(), and reject updatedAt values older than an application maximum age justified by that feed's documented behavior. Read through the current proxy on the intended network and define circuit-breaker or failure behavior. There is no safe universal heartbeat constant for every feed and application.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does read-only reentrancy specifically break an oracle consumer?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: The consumer prices collateral from a pool's view function (for example, Curve get_virtual_price) while an ETH refund during remove_liquidity has left pool balances and LP supply inconsistent. Historical Curve locks were not public, so integrations probed the lock by first calling a harmless lock-protected function and reverted if it was entered. Alternatively, use a source whose invariants hold during callbacks. Guarding only the consumer's entry point does not validate the external view.
